That $900 AmEx Platinum card does have a lot of perks. I don't have this card, but I have a friend who does, so I looked into it a bit. If you pay for streaming services and Uber regularly, you'll probably get half your fee back just on those, and then the other perks might get you close to all your money back if used smartly and if those purchases happen to coincide with things you'd be buying anyways.

The "catch" is that it is "only" 1% cash back, when there are some free cards that are 2% back now, so there is some meaningful opportunity cost. But if used strategically, likely for an upper middle income family (or high income family), the AmEx Platinum can be close to free *if* you use it only on things that get you big cash back and also don't use it to justify purchases you wouldn't have otherwise made.

comments.author: @JoshuaBost
comments.text:
I'm at least a little bit surpised you didn't mention Australia towards the end there.  There were highly relevant changes that occurred here last month, and I feel they would have been hard to miss while researching this.
On 1 October 2026 card surcharges were banned; interchange fees were capped, and in response at least a few credit card rewards schemes were gutted or cancelled outright since those interchange fees helped fund them.

The same sort of lobbying and scare tactics by credit cards happened here too, however, the thing about that is that we have regulators with a spine.
For the changes here it was the RBA and ACCC leading it - The ACCC is pretty much the final boss of Australian consumer protection. From what I can tell they have a bit of a reputation internationally, and are actually scary to global corporate giants.
The ACCC will happily take on the likes of Valve, Amazon, Google, Meta, Vokswagen, Uber, and Airbnb... to name a few; bringing the pain to them, sometimes to the betterment of everyone globally. The ACCC's landmark case against Valve is widely credited as a key driver for refunds on Steam.

So, despite the lobbying, the changes actually happened.  “A lot of the negative feedback I've seen is around the fact that at least some merchants chose to raise their sticker prices by more than the surcharge they were collecting.
It hasn't been long enough to really see the full effects of it, I'll be interested to see how this affects the airlines and their lounges over a longer period - though I expect that to be years.
For me personally I know that my credit card earning rewards for Qantas meant I would be WAY more likely to fly with them; but once the points I have access to are used they aren't going to replenish at any rate which really makes sense - so I'll probably drop both the card that led to it; as well as be more inclined to fly on other airlines.
